items.question: What real ground remains for doubt concerning one or two locations?
premises: Questions arise about where one is located
Questions arise about where two are located
Doubt presupposes distinct places or entities
items.inference: If no distinct locations can be established, doubt about one or two has no basis.
uncertainties: Exact vernacular forms and syntax are partly opaque
items.plain_english: Where is the one, where are the two? What doubt can there be?

items.question: How can doubt about coming and going persist after recognizing the self's oneness?
premises: The self's oneness is recognized by you
Coming and going imply division or movement between states
Recognition of oneness removes the basis for such division
items.inference: Therefore, once the self's oneness is known, doubt about coming and going cannot remain.
uncertainties: āvām is taken as coming-and-going based on context and hint
items.plain_english: If you have recognized the oneness of the self, then what doubt can remain about coming and going?

items.question: What meaningful distinction can be maintained among repeatedly identified alternatives?
premises: Multiple alternatives are presented in sequence
Each alternative is indicated as the same
Repeated identification collapses apparent difference
items.inference: All the presented alternatives are ultimately the same.
uncertainties: The referent of suha is not explicitly specified
items.plain_english: That or that or that or that—it is all the same.

items.question: Who can heal a person afflicted and weakened by the disease of worldly existence?
premises: The speaker is afflicted by the disease of worldly existence
The speaker is weak and in need of healing
Healing requires an effective remedy or healer
items.inference: The afflicted speaker calls for healing from the disease of worldly existence.
uncertainties: The intended healer is implicit rather than named
items.plain_english: Let him heal me, who am weak and afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.

rows.grounds: vernacular form for the earthly realm

items.question: Where have the earth and the three worlds merged upon dissolution?
premises: The earth and the three worlds are named
These realms are said to have merged
Merging raises the question of their locus
items.inference: The apparent worlds have no separate place once they are merged.
uncertainties: Vernacular forms gaiya, mīlitha, and katu are interpreted contextually
items.plain_english: Where have the earth, the realms of earth, atmosphere, and heaven all merged?

rows.grounds: compound: pṛthvī (earth) + ādi (beginning/et cetera), the elements starting with earth

items.question: Into what location does this entire world beginning with earth ultimately go?
premises: This world consists of earth and the other elements
The whole manifest totality is considered
Its going implies a destination or dissolution point
items.inference: The entire manifest world has no ascertainable separate destination.
items.plain_english: Where does all this, beginning with earth, go?

rows.grounds: compound: hi (like/as) + śīkhara (peak), simile marker with peak
compound: kṣi (perishable/decaying) + śīkhara (peak), peak of the perishable

items.question: How are the imperishable and the perishable related as peaks in appearance?
premises: The imperishable is described with the image of a peak
The perishable is also described with the image of a peak
A shared image suggests a relation or contrast
items.inference: The imperishable and perishable are presented through a common image that invites discernment of their relation.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic relation among the compounded forms is compressed
items.plain_english: The imperishable is like a peak, and the perishable is like a peak.

items.question: What harm can remain once the imperishable reality has been truly known?
premises: The imperishable can be known
Harm pertains to what is perishable or vulnerable
Knowledge of the imperishable removes vulnerability at that level
items.inference: If the imperishable is known, no real harm remains.
items.plain_english: If you have known that imperishable reality, then what harm can there be?

items.question: What remains when voidness itself has merged into the void?
premises: Voidness is distinguished as a state
That voidness is said to merge into the void
Merging implies the loss of a separate remainder
items.inference: When voidness merges into the void, no separate residue remains.
uncertainties: Vernacular endings in śūnyasa, śūnyāha, and gauva are interpreted from context
items.plain_english: Voidness has merged into the void and is gone.

rows.grounds: compound: cit (consciousness) + svarūpa (own-nature), essence as awareness

items.question: What reality remains when the distinction between seen and seer falls away?
premises: Experience is ordinarily divided into seen and seer
This verse states what remains after that division
What remains is identified as consciousness-nature
items.inference: Beyond the division of seen and seer, only consciousness-nature remains.
items.plain_english: When the seen and the seer are gone, what remains is consciousness itself.

rows.grounds: vernacular expression for the state of being dead

items.question: What kind of knowledge is attained by dying while still living?
premises: Living and having died are juxtaposed
The verse asks about a specific knowledge
The juxtaposition points to a paradoxical realization
items.inference: The verse points to a knowledge realized through dying to the ordinary self while alive.
uncertainties: The vernacular phrase mari-tāya is interpreted as having died
items.plain_english: What is that knowledge of one who has died while still living?

rows.grounds: the event or state of dying

items.question: Why can death never again apply to one who has already died in realization?
premises: The subject is described as already dead
Death is denied for that subject
The denial is made absolute by not ever
items.inference: For one who has truly died, death does not exist at any time.
uncertainties: Whether mṛtasya refers to physical or ego-death is context-dependent
items.plain_english: For one who is dead, there is indeed no death ever again.
